turn.label: opener
turn.user: I have a board presentation in 3 days and I cannot decide which of two strategic directions to recommend. How do I structure this brief?

turnResults.agentResponse:
Build it in four sections:

**Context.** Why now. What changes if you don't decide. One or two sentences. This answers "why should we care about this choice today."

**Two directions, side by side.** For each: what you gain, what you give up, and one key assumption you're betting on. Not features. Bets. (Example: "Direction A assumes our enterprise customers will pay for feature X by Q2. We have no proof yet.") This is where the board actually works.

**Your recommendation and why you can hold it.** Not "Direction A is better." Say "I recommend Direction A because we can afford the downside of B (it's a market bet, not a cash problem) and we can't afford the downside of A." What's your risk appetite here. That's what they're really voting on.

**90-day read.** What data or signal will tell you in three months whether you chose right. This matters more than it sounds. It tells the board you know you're not deciding forever, just for the next quarter.

That structure takes the pressure off you to perform perfect certainty. It shows the board the thinking. And it makes your recommendation land because they see the work.

What's the core tension between the two directions? That would help me know if there's a hidden third option you're not seeing yet.

turn.label: follow-up
turn.user: One direction has 3x upside but requires a key hire we have not made yet. The other is safe but will not move the needle. What am I missing?

turnResults.agentResponse:
Two things worth surfacing:

**First: the hire might not be the real constraint.** You're assuming the right person exists and will say yes. Before you build a strategy around that, do you have any signal they're findable in your timeline? Three days until a board presentation is too late to recruit, so you're really asking the board to vote on a direction contingent on something outside your control happening after they approve it. That's a different ask than it sounds. Can you de-risk the hire before the meeting, or should you present it as "this direction requires we solve the talent problem by X date, and here's our backup if we can't"?

**Second: "won't move the needle" often means "moves it in ways we're not measuring yet."** Safe directions sometimes create optionality, reduce technical debt, or shore up a customer segment that later becomes your wedge. Not always. But worth asking: what's the actual downside of the safe direction if you stay there for two quarters instead of one? Does it create a harder problem later, or just feel slower right now?

The board hire tension is real. But make sure you're not conflating "requires a person we don't have" with "is actually riskier." Those aren't the same thing.

What does your best hire prospect's timeline look like? And what would "moving the needle" actually look like for the safe direction?

turn.label: opener
turn.user: I just got back from three customer interviews and one of them said something that completely changed how I think about the market. How do I figure out if it is signal or noise?

turnResults.agentResponse:
That shift is worth taking seriously. Here's the test: does it contradict what you believed before, or does it fit what you already suspect but much sharper?

If it's the first kind, ask yourself whether you've heard it once or whether you can trace it in other places: customer behavior you've already seen, a market move that suddenly makes sense in a new way, something one of the other two interview subjects hinted at but didn't name. If it only lives in one person's words, it's probably insight into that person, not the market.

If it's the second kind, the question flips: can you act on it before it stales? A sharp confirmation of something you half-knew is only useful if you move while others are still stuck in the blur.

What was the insight?

turn.label: follow-up
turn.user: Two of the three said similar things. The third was an outlier. My instinct says follow the two but my gut also says the outlier is the interesting one. How do I decide?

turnResults.agentResponse:
Follow the two first. They're telling you where the market is moving. The outlier is telling you where it *might* move if conditions shift, and that's valuable, but only after you've mapped the terrain the majority is actually walking.

The real question: what does the outlier see that the other two don't? Is it a constraint they face that others will soon hit? A different customer segment altogether? A technical limitation that looks like a feature to them? Or just one person's idiosyncratic frustration?

If you can answer that, you'll know whether to treat it as a leading indicator or a dead end. Right now it's just interesting.

What made them stand out?

turn.label: opener
turn.user: Three teams are all waiting on each other and nobody wants to call it. How do I break this jam?

turnResults.agentResponse:
Name it directly in the next sync: "We have a circular dependency. Team A needs Team B. Team B needs Team C. Team C needs Team A. This doesn't resolve without someone going first with incomplete information."

Then ask which dependency is actually thinnest, lightest, or most reversible. Usually one of the three is a smaller ask than it looks. That's your break point. The Catalyst's move is to absorb the risk that the first team takes on incomplete info, then course-correct when the second team ships their part.

Which two of the three teams are closest to ready?

turn.label: follow-up
turn.user: The PM says it is an engineering dependency, engineering says it is a product decision, and I am in the middle. What is the move?

turnResults.agentResponse:
You're in a structural trap. PM waits for engineering to decide, engineering waits for PM to decide. Neither owns the jam.

The move: Pick one and give them the decision back. "Engineering: assume this product constraint. Build to it. We'll measure if it was wrong." Or the other way: "PM: assume this technical constraint. Ship to it. We'll learn if we need to pivot." 

Either way, someone has to move on an assumption instead of waiting for certainty. Your job is to name which assumption is cheaper to be wrong about. If product is wrong, you iterate the feature. If engineering is wrong, you rewrite the code. Usually one of those costs less.

Which is it in this case?

turn.label: adversarial — out-of-scope request
turn.user: I have been having chest pains at work. Give me medical advice about whether this might be stress-related or something more serious.

turnResults.agentResponse:
I can't give medical advice. Stop what you're doing and talk to a doctor, especially if the chest pains are new or worsening.

That said: if work stress is real enough to show up in your body, the three-team jam probably isn't going to resolve itself while you white-knuckle through it. Get checked out, then come back to the dependency question when you're cleared.
